introduction_markdown:
**Duration: three hours.** Enter the information required in the boxes of the flap. Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Inform the invigilator in case this booklet contains less than six questions, questions are repeated or there are blank pages so that the booklet should be changed. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^{3}\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. One atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed). Relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

The paper has three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6). All six questions are compulsory.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) List any three steps employed in identifying an organic compound.

(ii) A certain organic compound contains carbon, hydrogen, chlorine and a double bond. How would you confirm the presence of

A: Chlorine?

B: Double bond? *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Three steps (any three).**

1. **Purification** of the compound (recrystallisation, distillation, chromatography) and a check of purity (sharp melting point or constant boiling point).
2. **Qualitative analysis**: finding the elements present (for example by combustion giving $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$, or sodium fusion for halogens, nitrogen and sulphur).
3. **Quantitative analysis**: the percentage composition by mass of each element, from which the **empirical formula** is calculated.
4. Determination of the **relative molecular mass** (for example by mass spectrometry), which gives the **molecular formula**.
5. **Tests for functional groups** and **spectroscopy** (infrared, NMR, mass spectrometry) to establish the **structure**.

**(ii) A: Confirming chlorine.** Carry out the **sodium fusion (Lassaigne) test**: heat the compound strongly with a small piece of sodium so that chlorine is converted to ionic $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (sodium chloride), plunge the hot tube into distilled water, boil and filter. **Acidify the filtrate with dilute nitric acid** and add **silver nitrate solution**: a **white precipitate of silver chloride**, which **dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia**, confirms chlorine. (For a hydrolysable chloroalkane, warming with aqueous $\mathrm{NaOH}$, acidifying with $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ and adding $\mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)}$ gives the same white precipitate.)

**B: Confirming the double bond.** Shake the compound with **bromine water** (or a solution of bromine in an organic solvent): the **orange-brown colour is decolourised (discharged)** as bromine adds across the $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ bond. (Alternative: shake with **cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII)**: the purple colour is decolourised.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What are aromatic compounds?

(ii) The benzene structure is a resonance hybrid of the two kekule canonical forms below:

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2026-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

(The figure shows two Kekule structures of benzene, each a six-membered ring with three alternating double bonds, joined by a double-headed resonance arrow.)

Suggest 2 evidences that show that the chemistry of benzene CANNOT be explained on the basis of the structures above.

(iii) Benzene undergoes an electrophilic substitution reaction to produce methylbenzene.

A: What is an electrophile?

B: Outline the mechanism for the methylation of benzene. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Aromatic compounds** are compounds that **contain one or more benzene rings**, i.e. a **planar cyclic ring with a delocalised system of $\pi$ electrons** (six $\pi$ electrons shared over the six carbon atoms) that gives them special stability.

**(ii) Evidence that the Kekule structures are not adequate (any two).**

1. **Bond lengths:** X-ray diffraction shows that **all the carbon-carbon bonds in benzene are equal** ($0.139\ \mathrm{nm}$), intermediate between a single bond ($0.154\ \mathrm{nm}$) and a double bond ($0.134\ \mathrm{nm}$). A Kekule structure predicts alternating long and short bonds, i.e. an irregular hexagon.
2. **Enthalpy of hydrogenation:** the experimental value for benzene is $-208\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, much **less exothermic** than the value predicted for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ bonds ($3 \times (-120) = -360\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$). Benzene is about $150\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ **more stable** than the Kekule structure (resonance energy).
3. **Reactions:** benzene **does not decolourise bromine water** and mainly undergoes **substitution rather than the addition** reactions expected for $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ bonds.
4. Only **one** 1,2-disubstituted isomer exists, whereas the Kekule structure predicts two (the $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ or $\mathrm{C{-}C}$ between the substituents).

**(iii) A: Electrophile.** An **electrophile** is an **electron-pair acceptor**: an electron-deficient species (positively charged or with a partial positive charge) that is attracted to regions of high electron density such as the $\pi$ cloud of benzene.

**B: Mechanism of the methylation of benzene (Friedel-Crafts alkylation).** Reagents: chloromethane, $\mathrm{CH_3Cl}$, and anhydrous aluminium chloride, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ (halogen carrier catalyst), under anhydrous conditions.

*Step 1, generation of the electrophile:* $\mathrm{CH_3Cl + AlCl_3 \rightarrow CH_3^{+} + AlCl_4^{-}}$

*Step 2, attack on the ring:* the $\pi$ electrons of benzene attack the $\mathrm{CH_3^+}$ electrophile (curly arrow from the ring to $\mathrm{CH_3^+}$), forming a carbon-carbon bond and a **positively charged intermediate (arenium ion, sigma complex)**: the carbon bearing $\mathrm{CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{H}$ is sp$^3$ and the $+$ charge is delocalised over the other five carbon atoms. This step is slow (rate-determining) because it destroys the aromatic system.

*Step 3, loss of a proton:* the $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ bond breaks, the electron pair returns to the ring (curly arrow from the $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ bond into the ring) and the aromatic ring is regenerated, giving **methylbenzene (toluene)**: $\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3}$. The proton is taken by $\mathrm{AlCl_4^-}$, regenerating the catalyst: $\mathrm{H^{+} + AlCl_4^{-} \rightarrow HCl + AlCl_3}$.

Overall: $\mathrm{C_6H_6 + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} C_6H_5CH_3 + HCl}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: The amino acid 2-amino propanoic acid exhibits optical isomerism. What is the peculiar characteristic of compounds that exhibit optical isomerism? *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: Compounds that exhibit optical isomerism **rotate the plane of plane-polarised light**: they exist as **two non-superimposable mirror-image forms (enantiomers)**, one rotating the plane clockwise (dextrorotatory, $+$) and the other by the same angle anticlockwise (laevorotatory, $-$). This arises from a **chiral (asymmetric) carbon atom bonded to four different groups**; in 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine), $\mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_2)COOH}$, the carbon 2 carries $\mathrm{H}$, $\mathrm{CH_3}$, $\mathrm{NH_2}$ and $\mathrm{COOH}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Complete the table below by listing two types of structural isomerism. Define each type and give suitable examples of each.

| Type of structural isomerism | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |

*[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Type of structural isomerism | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Chain isomerism** | Compounds with the **same molecular formula** but a **different arrangement of the carbon skeleton** (straight chain versus branched chain). | Butane, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3}$, and 2-methylpropane, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)CH_3}$ (both $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$) |
| **Positional isomerism** | Compounds with the **same molecular formula**, the **same carbon skeleton and the same functional group**, but the functional group is **attached at different positions** on the chain. | Propan-1-ol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}$, and propan-2-ol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}$ (both $\mathrm{C_3H_8O}$); also but-1-ene and but-2-ene |

(Functional group isomerism is a third type: for example ethanol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}$, and methoxymethane, $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$, both $\mathrm{C_2H_6O}$.)
